questions.stem: Jessica, 26, is back at the GP for her results. Her bloods, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin and stool tests are all normal. You explain that irritable bowel syndrome is the likely diagnosis. She looks upset and asks, "So is this all in my head?" What is the best response?
options: No. Your symptoms are real; gut and brain signal abnormally, and stress can worsen it
Your tests are all normal, so there is nothing physically wrong with your bowel right now
Stress is the main cause, so seeing a psychologist is the key treatment for you
We can't be sure what it is until a colonoscopy has ruled out something serious
questions.why: IBS should be explained as a positive diagnosis: a real, common disorder of gut-brain interaction (visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility) that stress can worsen, and that does not damage the bowel or cause cancer.
notes: Saying 'nothing is wrong' dismisses real symptoms, makes her feel disbelieved and does nothing to build trust in the diagnosis.
Stress makes it worse but does not fully explain it, and psychological therapy is one part of management, not the whole treatment.
She has no red flags and a normal calprotectin, so colonoscopy is not indicated, and suggesting it adds to her fear of cancer.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, has 2 months of crampy lower abdominal pain, alternating loose and hard stools, and bloating. She has no rectal bleeding, weight loss or night symptoms, and no family history. FBC, ferritin, CRP and coeliac serology are normal, stool PCR is negative, and faecal calprotectin is 28 µg/g. What is the most appropriate next step in general practice?
options: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude microscopic colitis and early IBD, with biopsies
Repeat faecal calprotectin in 6 weeks before making any diagnosis
No colonoscopy; working IBS diagnosis with GP review in 4 to 6 weeks
Request CT abdomen and pelvis to exclude a structural cause
questions.why: A calprotectin below 50 µg/g in a young adult with no red flags makes IBD unlikely and means no colonoscopy is needed. Make a positive working IBS diagnosis, start treatment and review in 4 to 6 weeks to confirm it.
notes: Colonoscopy is for red flags or a raised calprotectin. Microscopic colitis mostly affects older people, and she has neither.
A repeat test is for a borderline or raised result. 28 µg/g is clearly normal, and holding back the diagnosis delays treatment.
CT adds radiation and finds incidental lesions without a clinical question to answer; her examination and tests do not suggest a structural cause.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, says her bloating, wind and loose stools are worse after a lot of dairy. She drinks milk-based bubble tea most days. She has a history of bee sting anaphylaxis. What mechanism best explains why dairy brings on her symptoms?
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the gut mucosa in response to cow's milk protein
Low brush-border lactase: lactose reaches colon, draws in water and is fermented to gas
Deficient pancreatic lactase secretion leaves lactose undigested in the small bowel lumen
Milk fat triggers excess bile acid release, which stimulates colonic water secretion
questions.why: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme of small bowel enterocytes. When it is low, undigested lactose pulls water into the lumen (osmotic diarrhoea), and colonic bacteria ferment it to hydrogen, CO2 and short-chain fatty acids, which causes bloating and wind.
notes: IgE cow's milk allergy causes rapid urticaria, vomiting or anaphylaxis, not dose-related bloating. Her bee sting allergy does not make it likely.
Lactase is not a pancreatic enzyme; it sits on the small bowel brush border, so pancreatic insufficiency does not cause lactose intolerance.
Bile acid diarrhoea follows ileal disease or cholecystectomy and does not explain sugar fermentation, gas or the link with dose of milk.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, cannot pinpoint her crampy pain and gestures vaguely around her umbilicus and lower abdomen. Pain from distension of midgut-derived bowel (distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) is usually referred to which region?
options: Epigastrium, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T6 to T8
Suprapubic region, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T12 to L1
Perineum, via visceral afferents travelling with pelvic splanchnics at S2 to S4
Periumbilical region, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T10
questions.why: Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres to the cord segments that supplied the embryonic gut tube, bilaterally and across several levels, so pain is vague and midline. Midgut pain is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus.
notes: Epigastric referral is for foregut structures such as the stomach, proximal duodenum, liver and gallbladder.
Suprapubic (hypogastric) referral is for hindgut structures from the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum, not the midgut.
Pelvic splanchnic afferents carry pain from the lower rectum and pelvic organs, not from distension of midgut bowel.
